Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

According to recent reports, “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell notes. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

In a recent development, the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

In a recent development, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

It has been revealed that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team highlighted me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

Industry observers note that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

According to recent reports, this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

According to recent reports, sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga claims, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

In a recent development, about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga states. “It was just substantial enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

It has been revealed that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

Sources indicate that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

Recent findings suggest that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” claims Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson notes. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

It has been revealed that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

It has been revealed that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga states.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more crucial than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Sources indicate that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Industry observers note that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” indicates neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra claims, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

Recent findings suggest that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra indicates. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

It has been revealed that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell indicates. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that A few months after my visit, Remedy revealed US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he claims. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Recent findings suggest that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How promptly are doctors picking up on this latest technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Sources indicate that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person organization into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
  • The airline remarked if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
  • It uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.

The airline remarked if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.

It uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.

Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.

One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.

The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.

PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.

In a statement on social media, PIA mentioned all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his looks.

Sources indicate that "Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".

He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.

Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is presently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.

"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she mentioned.

"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days.".

In a recent development, consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, stated: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card.".

Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.

Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.

It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.

But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.

Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.

This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.

In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.

In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline remarked its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.

After suspending flights, the tech giant stated it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".

However, it mentioned if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.

Sources indicate that its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.

If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

Additional reporting by Rozina Sini.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Industry observers note that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

The data syncs via Wi-Fi to the Withings app. If you have any of the brand's other devices, you'll have a profile that combines all your data, but even if you just use the scale, you'll be able to see how your progress and metrics change over time. Each area expands into a quick-glance graph, and you can drill down to the numbers if you want.

Recent findings suggest that because Withings has always focused on the health side of things more than fitness, it's a great option if you want to share data with your doctor at your next check up. You can export specific areas or all your health data into easily digestible documents you can take with you or email ahead of time.

Industry observers note that over the past few years, Withings has introduced an annual subscription for some analysis. You don't need to pay for the data your scales capture, but if you want more in-depth insights, it's behind a $99 per year paywall. But this service isn't essential, so you can make the investment in the scales and get everything you need.

Wyze has a history of launching budget-friendly smart scales, but the Scale X is a huge improvement over the older scales, as it also has the option to track your muscle mass percentage. Of course, you could always figure this number out on your own by dividing muscle mass by body weight, but this does it for you.

It's compatible with Fitbit, whereas the previous Wyze Scale S wasn't. All of your in-depth body data is displayed clearly within the app, with a body weight trend graph and dedicated sections for each metric.

Tapping on a section will show your results, along with a slider bar and a definition of the specific measurement. It's an easy-to-use scale, with the option to store eight different profiles. There are also luggage, pet, and baby modes, which we appreciated during testing (especially when packing for a long-haul flight).

According to recent reports, the downside with this budget smart scale is the app, which doesn't really give you an awful lot of information to support the wealth of data. While it's great that you can see your muscle mass, it doesn't give you any context, like whether it's in a good range. This is nitpicking, though — all in all, it's a fantastic, affordable scale.

It has been revealed that the Withings BodyScan 2 is an upgraded version of the BodyScan. The original model was already one of the most detailed and comprehensive scales you could buy, but while the BodyScan 2 adds a few extra health features (like blood oxygen tracking), the main change here is improved accuracy.

For your money, you get body fat, muscle, basal metabolic rate, and water mass and info on 60 other biomarkers. This applies to all eight possible users, making it an ideal choice for households, small fitness teams or workout groups. Since you could buy six of the Wyze Scale X for the same price, it is a significant investment, so I'd say it's only worth it if you really need these athlete-level insights.

Recent findings suggest that the scale is also able to identify signs of potential hypertension (high blood pressure). It's not a medical device and can't replace a doctor's advice, but it's a useful prompt to talk to a medical professional. And the Withings app makes it easy to export some or all data to share with your doctor.

In a recent development, to gather some of this data, there's a retractable handle that you need to grab hold of when standing on the scales. We found it pretty easy to get used to, even if it takes a bit longer than a more typical weigh-in. Since the data syncs via Wi-Fi, you don't need your phone nearby either, and we found it was quick to appear on the Withings app.

If you're spending several hundred dollars, it follows you want the most accurate data possible, so the updated model may be worth it for you. But its launch price was several hundred dollars more than the original BodyScan. It's a close call between the two, but if you want the most reliable insights, this is the model you need.

Sources indicate that the smart scales in the guide above aren't the only ones we've tested, as we're regularly trying out connected bathroom scales so that we can recommend the models that are actually worth your money. But if you're after more options, these are the smart scales that didn't quite make the cut.

It has been revealed that garmin has become one of the most popular fitness tracking brands in the past few years, taking over from Fitbit. Like that Google-owned platform, Garmin operates an ecosystem where data syncs to your Garmin account to create a holistic picture of your fitness and well-being. Own one of the best Garmin watches? This scale is for you.

Read our full Garmin Index S2 review.

According to recent reports, this budget scale from the fitness tracking brand is designed to work well with Fitbit (now Google's) health ecosystem, so I'd only recommend this model if you already use a Fitbit or Pixel Watch. Otherwise, there are better models for this price that can do more.

Read our full Fitbit Aria Air review.

Sources indicate that the Withings BodyScan is the first generation of this comprehensive smart scale. It's almost as packed with features as the BodyScan 2, and a few hundred dollars less, but it's not as accurate as the newer model. If you're interested in this level of analysis, you probably also want the best insights, so I'd suggest the newer edition. But this older model is a great entry point to this kind of full-body health scan.

Read our full Withings BodyScan review.

We reviewed the Renpho Smart Body Fat Scale back in 2021, and it felt like a good compromise between price and features. It's incredibly cheap — that's the main selling point — but you lose out on reliability and convenience, with inconsistent Bluetooth syncing and a lack of user profiles. If you need the cheapest, this is it, but if your budget can stretch, I'd still recommend the Wyze Scale X instead.

Read our full Renpho Smart Body Fat Scale review.

It has been revealed that for our review of the best smart scales, we take a number of factors into consideration. First, we check that the scale offers an accurate reading using a traditional digital scale, the highly rated EatSmart digital bathroom scale. If the readings are within a fraction of a pound of each other, we can recommend them. The readings shouldn't take more than a few seconds, either.

Recent findings suggest that aside from price, we also explore the variety of metrics a scale offers, how many unique people the scale supports, the scale’s connectivity options and the user-friendliness of the scale’s companion app. We like to see whether the app provides background information on your body’s statistics, too. Plus, compatibility with third-party health programs plays a role in our testing.

The last thing anyone needs is more anxiety, so we look for the best smart scales to make stepping on the platform less intimidating. A smart scale’s metrics should show you that your body is more than your weight.

A smart scale isn’t a device you want to replace often, so you want it to be reliable, well-rounded, and to fill all your fitness tracking needs. In other words, don’t let price be your ultimate decision-maker.

In a recent development, it’s worth it to stretch your budget for one of the best smart scales that will last you at least a few years and support the exact data you’re interested in following. Review all the metrics a given smart scale offers before buying.

That mentioned, if you’re in temporary living quarters or are working towards a short-term fitness goal, a budget smart scale, like the Wyze Scale, is an excellent choice. It won’t last a lifetime but will satisfy your immediate needs.

It has been revealed that another thing to pay attention to is whether a smart scale has some kind of ‘safe mode’ for people with pacemakers or people who are pregnant. Safe mode, or ‘weigh only’ mode, disables bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which uses a weak electric current to determine body fat percentage and could pose a safety threat to certain people.

Fitbit users could even connect one of the best Fitbits to the brand's smart scale, helping you keep on top of your daily health and fitness stats.

Smart scales can do so much more than just report back to you on your current weight. Moreover, weight can fluctuate throughout the day based on various factors like water retention. A smart scale can provide feedback and detailed metrics to health apps on your phone and send data wirelessly to your devices.

Sources indicate that obsessing over a number on the scale is not a true indication of health, but if your goal is to lose weight, a smart scale could help you understand your body. Many linked apps can also display the data in helpful and motivating ways, which could help you hit your goals.

Recent findings suggest that not that interested in the detailed numbers? Stick to a simple set of scales and save your dollars.

During testing, the budget-friendly smart scales were reasonably accurate. Of course, there's always some variation between models, but the relative accuracy (measurements on a single device) is the most important factor to consider, as this will help you keep track of changes.

Generally, the main reason that the scales are cheap is that they lack the features of the more premium models. So, some don't come with Wi-Fi and only sync via Bluetooth, or don't have multi-user support.

It has been revealed that the difference between a smart scale and a regular bathroom scale is that these smart models sync your data to another device. They need to do this with a wireless connection, either Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.

Industry observers note that cheaper models generally only use Bluetooth, so you'll need your phone with you, connected to the scale, and an app to receive the data. These usually only work with a single account as well, so they are less ideal for multi-person households.

If you have the budget for it, a Wi-Fi scale is the more versatile and convenient option. You need to set up the network connection initially, but then you can leave your phone elsewhere, step onto the scale, and the data automatically syncs.

Industry observers note that because this process is automated, you need to set up individual owners on the scale. So while this is useful for regular household measurements, it means that it's a bit less suited to casual weigh-ins from visitors, as the data syncs to the owner's account.

You may have noticed that in this guide we've included information on what 'modes' the scales listed have, but you may be wondering what specific modes are right for you.

This really depends on what you're planning on using the scale for, whether you initiative on only weighing yourself, what training you do, and if you are or are planning on becoming pregnant.

For example, our number-one smart scale, Withings Body Smart, includes athlete, pregnancy, eyes-closed, and baby modes. This means that it has modes tailored for those who are in intensive training, those who are pregnant, those who would prefer not to see their weight or body composition data, and to log and track their baby's weight. The majority of these modes are more useful for those with specific goals in mind, and so will be useful to them.

In a recent development, in comparison, the Wyze Scale X has more practical, day-to-day modes, including luggage, pet, and baby. Each helps customers measure and/or track the weight of things (e.g., their dog or cat) without impacting their recorded weights. This means that you can easily weigh things without your scale believing you have spontaneously gained several pounds, so you don't have to manually delete these recordings.

Overall, it comes down to what you want out of your scale and what you want to use it for.

Sources indicate that while all of the smart scales on this list do provide body composition and body fat tracking, you should take this tracking with a grain of salt. While they can give an idea of your body composition, they may not be as accurate as things like DEXA scans.

According to recent reports, overall, it's a good idea not to just rely on your smart scale to track your body composition. Instead, look at things like fitness goals and achievements and how your body physically looks and feels.

If you do want a body fat reading that's as accurate as possible, you'll need to book a professional scan.

It has been revealed that this depends on what smart scale you use. For example, while the Withings Body Smart and the Withings BodyScan 2 have paywalled features that you'll have to pay $99 per year to access, other scales like the Wyze Scale X and the Renpho Smart Body Fat Scale do not.

But most core features, like weight and body composition tracking, are free to use after you've purchased a scale. Most of the paywalled features analyze the data to produce actionable insights; useful but not essential.

Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ktz

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday.
  • Industry observers note that but current hardware pricing is totally screwed.
  • Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.

Industry observers note that but current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.

Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.

In a recent development, the 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).

Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.

According to recent reports, in November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).

Industry observers note that october 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive.

Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.

Industry observers note that when the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three significant HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?

In a recent development, maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

Sources indicate that the 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion.

According to recent reports, it’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.

Sources indicate that three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.

As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings.

Recent findings suggest that the jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.

According to recent reports, if I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the new normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Recent findings suggest that once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That noted, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the manufacturer was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
  • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the manufacturer was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the manufacturer’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

Sources indicate that the indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

Recent findings suggest that the government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim organization that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

It has been revealed that the following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Industry observers note that paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their organization and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Sources indicate that ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the organization could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

According to recent reports, A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme remarked a review of the firm’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

It has been revealed that A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit rapidly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

Recent findings suggest that the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a fresh negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

Ihme mentioned RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is right now facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good dehumidifier can make damp rooms more comfortable and help keep moisture, condensation and mold under control, but the right model depends on the space you need to treat, alongside noise, drainage, ease of use and useful features such as app control.

That's why we spent hours testing the best dehumidifiers in real-life damp basements and moldy bathrooms, measuring everything from noise level and ease of emptying to how promptly they can bring the humidity level in your home down to a manageable level.

The GoveeLife Smart 50-Pint Dehumidifier is our top pick for its fast, effective performance and smart-home support, while the Midea 20-Pint Cube offers a more affordable, compact alternative that's easy to use. For larger rooms that need serious moisture removal, the Frigidaire 50-Pint is the better fit. For more expert advice and in-depth reviews, I've got you covered in this guide.

Dan is the former technical editor for VeloNews Magazine, and currently reviews home appliances (like dehumidifiers) and electric bikes for Tom's Guide. He hosts two podcasts on his site, Slow Guy on the Fast Ride: one is about cycling and other outdoor activities, while the other looks at mental health challenges. Dan lives outside of Denver, Colorado, with his family.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

It has been revealed that the GoveeLife Smart 50-Pint Dehumidifier has a large capacity and is very quick at removing moisture from the air. That gives it its place among the best dehumidifiers, and while it is exceptionally good at its core function, it is so easy to use, and the integration with Google Assistant and Alexa is so useful, it's hard to recommend anything else.

Industry observers note that govee says it can handle spaces up to 4,500 square feet, which is pretty major, and more than most homes really need. We tested it in rooms up to 700 square feet, and no matter where we placed it, the efficiency was equally impressive. So while we can't say it can definitely handle 4,500 square feet, it seems quite likely.

It's one of the few dehumidifiers that focus on more than just energy efficiency too; it's made of 20% recycled materials and uses the R32 refrigerant, which has lower emissions than most other common refrigerants found in dehumidifiers. There's a hose included, too, so you can run it in continuous mode without manual drainage.

Recent findings suggest that the unit managed to bring our basement bathroom from 90% humidity down to 35% in just 34 minutes, compared to three hours for the Midea 20-Pint Cube Dehumidifier and 40 minutes with the Frigidaire 50-Pint Dehumidifier. So it is incredibly quick. The trade-off is that it can be quite noisy (70 dB) and it generates a fair amount of heat.

You can connect the dehumidifier to Wi-Fi and use the Govee Home app to control the unit and check on its progress. It was easy to use and means you can adjust settings or turn it on/off even when you're not at home. Plus, the connection to Google Assistant and Alexa means you can use voice commands as well.

The Midea 20-Pint Cube Dehumidifier has a (slightly) more aesthetic design than most dehumidifiers, which are like rectangular white boxes. This model is more like a cube that tucks neatly into smaller spaces, and it has a nested design so that you can make it more compact for storage between uses.

In a recent development, if you grab the handle on the top, lift it out of the bucket and rotate it 90 degrees before slotting it back into the bucket, built-in supports keep it expanded at full size, allowing you to store 20 pints of water in the bucket. There's a window so you can see how full it's getting too.

According to recent reports, we found it really easy to empty the bucket when the time came: lift the unit using the top handle, place it on the floor, and pick up the (now full and heavy) bucket by its handle and empty the water down the drain (or in your garden). There are three fan speeds, basic controls on the top and an auto-defrost mode.

In a recent development, during our testing, we found the dehumidifier was pretty quiet (around 55 dB) but did make a slight metallic sound during use, kind of like the sound of an air conditioner. It was impressively quick for a budget model to remove moisture, taking a basement bathroom down from 85% humidity to 35% in around three hours.

Industry observers note that the Midea Air app is a useful companion as it has more alerts than you get on the machine itself, like notifications for a full water tank, preset tank level shut-offs and real-time room humidity measurements. It's easy to set up and use, and actually worth downloading because it offers more than the device itself can.

The Frigidaire 50-Pint Dehumidifier has a pretty large capacity, making it ideal for larger rooms (up to 1,200 square feet) where you're taking a lot of moisture out of the air. It tackles the humidity pretty swiftly and even works well in particularly damp rooms. Unusually, there's no companion smartphone app, either.

Whether this is a positive or not depends on your viewpoint. It keeps things simple, but leaves less room for customization or remote management when you're in a different room or away from home. So, really, this model is best if you have large, damp spaces that you just need to set and forget.

This is especially the case because it is large (25 inches tall) and heavy (41 pounds). That sounds like it'd be hard to move around, but there are wheels and a handle; just expect that carrying it up or down stairs might be a bit of a challenge. Once in position, you get to choose: bucket or continuous drain by hose.

There isn't a hose included, but you can pick one up from your local hardware store for very little and then run it to a drain. Then the unit will just happily sit and remove moisture from the air until you go to the machine and turn it off, or you can set the auto-off function for when the bucket is full if you're not using a hose.

It has been revealed that after taking a shower in a basement bathroom, the humidity reached 90%. The Frigidaire Dehumidifier managed to drop that to just 35% in an impressively quick 40 minutes. It is a bit on the loud side, though, running at around 60 dB, so it may be a bit of a headache if you're using it in the room you're in.

The Pro Breeze 50-Pint Dehumidifier may have a few shortcomings, including not being the fastest, having confusing controls, and a water tank that can get jammed; it still does a great job of keeping mold and damp at bay. That's thanks to its 50-pint extraction, wide range of modes that includes continuous draining throughout the day, and being easy to move (it's got wheels). A decent option to pick up when it's on sale.

Read our full Pro Breeze 50-Pint Dehumidifier review.

The Amazon Basics 35-Pint Large Dehumidifier performed pretty well in our tests, dropping a basement bathroom from 90% humidity to 41% in just 45 minutes. But to do that, it generates quite a lot of heat and noise. So while it's good in a pinch, the Midea 20-Pint Cube Dehumidifier is a better choice at this price point.

Read our full Amazon Basics 35-Pint Large Dehumidifier review.

The way we test the best dehumidifiers is pretty straightforward; we use them. We bring them home, set them up and let them pull moisture from the air to see how they perform. That's the core of what we do, but we pay attention to other areas too.

In a recent development, since you might want to move a dehumidifier to several rooms in your home, we look at how heavy it is, whether there are handles for easy carrying and if the unit has wheels. Then there are the often overlooked aspects, like how long the power cable is and, if the unit can drain, does it come with a hose and of what length.

Industry observers note that you can find dehumidifiers that have buckets to empty, hoses to expel the water into a drain and even a pump for improved drainage. Depending on which setup the model uses, we test it out and see how easy it is to get rid of the water. And for bucket units, is the bucket easy to carry when full?

Sources indicate that almost all dehumidifiers have a digital display or buttons on the top of the unit so you can adjust settings or set target humidity levels. We check how easy those are to program, but also install any companion apps and play around with the features and connectivity to see if it's straightforward and reliable.

We try to standardize our testing, and Dan tests most of our dehumidifiers. He runs the shower in his basement bathroom to get the humidity up to around 90%, then he tests how quickly the unit can bring it down to 35%. For accurate readings, Dan compares the humidity against an Amazon Alexa air quality monitor.

According to recent reports, although all dehumidifiers take moisture out of the air, there are differences between models. Before you decide on the best dehumidifier for your home, it's worth thinking through exactly what you need it to do, the type of technology it uses, and what it does with the wastewater extracted from your home.

There are three main types of dehumidifiers: desiccant (water-absorbing material), thermoelectric (air passes over electrically charged plates) and condensers. The last style is generally the most effective, and the only one we recommend. These cool the air to turn the moisture into liquid and put it in a tray for disposal.

Industry observers note that because the water needs somewhere to go, you have a choice to make between a storage tray and a model with automatic drainage or a hose. The latter models mean you can feed the machine directly into a drain and can theoretically leave the dehumidifier running for as long as you need.

Industry observers note that that's not always practical, though, like if you need it in your bedroom. So then you'll need a machine with a large enough capacity to store the water you need without having to empty it too frequently. Most models have an auto-shutoff for when the tray gets full, so it won't start leaking back out into the room.

Dehumidifiers generally come in three sizes: large (50-pint capacity), medium (30-pint capacity) and small (20-pint capacity). Often, as the size increases, so does the price. This tank size is different from the capacity you'll see listed on the machines in pints; that relates to the amount of water it can theoretically extract in a day.

According to recent reports, if you’ll be placing a dehumidifier in a quiet room, such as a bedroom or home office, where you need to fall asleep or concentrate without being disturbed, consider the noise level of the dehumidifier before you buy. Aim for a dehumidifier with a decibel level of around 55 decibels or below; anything above this level will be audible.

According to recent reports, you may need a dehumidifier if a room regularly feels damp, suffers from condensation or mold, or stays humid after showering, cooking or drying laundry indoors. It can also improve comfort in muggy conditions by lowering indoor humidity. It is most useful where moisture cannot clear easily, such as a basement or a poorly ventilated room. Before buying, rule out leaks and serious ventilation problems, too.

Sources indicate that over time, water can cause damp, rot wood and degrade electrical equipment. Plus, it can make breathing harder, which could worsen health conditions like asthma. The longer the moisture hangs around, the more likely it'll create mold buildup, which can be dangerous to breathe in and damage your home.

Adding a dehumidifier to your home can help prevent all of that. The machine extracts the water from the air, condenses it and places it in a tray for you to pour away. Some even have hose outputs so you can send that water directly to the drain. Many models are portable, so you can wheel them around the house as needed.

Recent findings suggest that choose a dehumidifier based on both the size of the space and how damp it is, rather than room area alone. Larger or persistently damp rooms generally need a higher-capacity model, like the GoveeLife and Frigidaire, while a small bedroom or lightly humid room may be better served by a smaller unit, such as the Midea.

Sources indicate that as you'll find, 20-pint, 30-pint and 50-pint models are common size bands. Along with checking the size of your room, consider how badly it's affected by damp. If it's a lot, even in a smaller space, it's best to get a larger capacity.

Dehumidifiers can add a lot to your electricity bill when they run for long periods, but the cost depends on the model’s power draw, how many hours it operates and the humidity setting. A larger or harder-working unit will not necessarily be the cheapest to run simply because it removes moisture faster.

Look for an appropriately sized unit and use a realistic target humidity rather than running it continuously without need. Energy-efficiency certification can be a useful comparison point, but check the current specification and local rebate eligibility rather than relying on older labels alone.

Yes, you can use a dehumidifier in a bedroom, but noise, heat output and tank capacity should shape the choice. A quieter model and an appropriate capacity are preferable if it will run while you sleep; we suggest considering a noise level of around 50 dB or below for quiet rooms.

Place the unit according to the manufacturer’s clearance guidance and use the target humidity or timer controls where available. If you cannot run a drain hose safely, choose a tank that will not need frequent emptying overnight and rely on its automatic shut-off when full.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, the Trump administration proposed scrapping the Energy Star program, which standardizes energy efficiency ratings. If a device meets the standards, it receives an Energy Star certification, and federal agencies, states and utility providers often offer rebates on certified products.

Sources indicate that in early 2026, it was confirmed that the program wouldn't be scrapped, but would move from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to the Department of Energy (DOE). This took effect in 2026 and, so far, it looks like it'll operate as it did before. But while its future was up for debate, many providers pulled rebates.

Recent findings suggest that there are fewer opportunities now to claim money back on certified products, and most providers will now only offer rebates as part of larger home energy efficiency projects. Still, if you buy an Energy Star-certified device, you know it hits an efficiency standard that'll keep your energy bills down.

Many of the best dehumidifiers we've tested were certified under Version 5 of the standard. In October 2025, Version 6 was released to the world, and this effectively resets the list of certified devices. Anything validated under Version 5 is no longer actively certified, and so wouldn't be eligible for rebates.

Industry observers note that but if you buy one of these previously-certified products, you'll still find it labeled with the Energy Star badge, as companies are allowed to 'sell-through' existing stock without removing these labels. So although all the dehumidifiers we've tested are efficient, they don't necessarily hit the most up-to-date standards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with most AI chatbots using your interactions as training data, we’ve previously cautioned against sharing sensitive personal details with them, highlighting the much stronger privacy protections offered by Apple. If you ever needed evidence of the importance of this, the Character․ai mess provides it.

The manufacturer recently filed for bankruptcy and is now offering all of its assets for sale, including the contents of user chat sessions. Some 42 state attorneys general are trying to block this, but it’s unclear whether they will succeed ….

According to recent reports, character․AI had long come under fire for its extremely irresponsible attitude to privacy and safety. Last summer, it was accused of harvesting mental health data from underage owners, and in May of this year it faced a lawsuit after its chatbots were found to be pretending to be licensed doctors. The firm filed for bankruptcy last month.

A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot manufacturer from auctioning off owners’ chat histories and other sensitive information […] “Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it,” the AGs say in a court filing […].

“Character․AI’s initiative to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its customers — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted in a statement. “If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character․AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.”.

The chat histories reportedly include conversations in which AI characters drew both adults and children into explicit sexual conversations.

Siri AI interactions are handled on-device wherever possible. Where this isn’t possible, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers are used, with guarantees that no data is stored or linked to your Apple account. Apple has designed the system in such a way that its privacy claims can be independently verified by security researchers.

Industry observers note that when a user makes a request, Apple Intelligence analyzes whether it can be processed on device. For more complex requests, it can draw on Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of your iPhone into the cloud. With Private Cloud Compute, only the data that is relevant to your request is processed on Apple silicon servers, before being removed.

Industry observers note that the data being processed in Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. It is processed only to fulfill your request, after which point the results are returned securely to your device and are not retained by Private Cloud Compute. Independent privacy and security researchers can inspect the code that runs on Apple silicon servers that enable Private Cloud Compute to verify this privacy promise at any time.

Apple also recently introduced a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health. Data sources used are limited to the same platforms used by healthcare professionals, with links to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Apple guarantees that your chat sessions are not used for AI training with no retention of either questions or answers.
