📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation.
  • US bill to tighten controls on chipmaking equipment sales to China goes “way too far”, Dutch trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma told parliament on Thursday, according to Reuters.
  • The minister stated the proposal could put Europe at an unacceptable disadvantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation.

US bill to tighten controls on chipmaking equipment sales to China goes “way too far”, Dutch trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma told parliament on Thursday, according to Reuters.

The minister stated the proposal could put Europe at an unacceptable disadvantage. His warning targets the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, or MATCH Act, which the US Congress is negotiating to attach to its annual defence policy bill.

The Dutch government has been lobbying against the bipartisan proposal for months. Under the bill, US allies with major semiconductor industries, including the Netherlands and Japan, would have 150 days to bring their export controls on China into line with Washington’s. If they did not, the US would impose restrictions on their equipment makers itself.

That would land hardest on ASML, the Dutch company whose lithography machines are essential for making advanced chips, and Europe’s most valuable listed firm.

The government opposes the bill’s extraterritorial reach, Sjoerdsma noted, and the damage would not stop at the Dutch border, because other European countries’ chip industries would also be hit.

“We will not simply be told what to do. If the act is adopted, our message to the US administration will be to not enforce it,” Sjoerdsma stated.

Industry observers note that he also pointed to the stakes for the region’s AI ambitions, telling parliament that Europe cannot afford to fall behind in semiconductors. Sjoerdsma mentioned he was in close contact with his European colleagues about a common response to the bill.

In a recent development, the remarks are a sharp turn in a relationship that has mostly bent to US pressure. The Netherlands criticised US restrictions in 2023 but still introduced its own controls on ASML’s advanced machines that year, and has tightened them several times since.

ASML’s former chief executive Peter Wennink argued in 2024 that the ever-expanding export curbs were driven more by US economics than by security. China was once ASML’s second-largest market, and the restrictions have already cut its sales there.

Whether the MATCH Act becomes law now depends on the defence bill negotiations in Congress, where lawmakers are deciding which provisions make it into the final text. No date has been set for a vote, which leaves the Dutch government time to press its case in Washington.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place.
  • The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.

As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.

The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.

Some examples of these fresh inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc….

These new forks generally all have a few things in common:.

Industry observers note that … and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model, on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.

In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster.

In a recent development, strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.

That mentioned, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.

Sources indicate that enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts. It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.

In a recent development, if you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.

podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1.

This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:.

My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines.

I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet.

On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled:.

In a recent development, strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.

Industry observers note that * It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo.

Sources indicate that unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

In a recent development, the MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

In a recent development, there are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Sources indicate that still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

The MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is at the moment on sale with a starting price of $999.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

As I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

Recent findings suggest that the M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

In a recent development, one of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

In a recent development, beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

In a recent development, if it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

Switzerland confirms first AI agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that attackers are now using AI agents against companies and critical infrastructure operators in Switzerland.
  • “In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems,” the agency wrote.
  • Florian Schütz, the NCSC’s director, gave the first figures on Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Verzasca Dam in Ticino, Switzerland.

Industry observers note that attackers are now using AI agents against companies and critical infrastructure operators in Switzerland. The country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) confirmed its first such cyberattacks in an advisory on Tuesday. The federal agency said the attacks hit at least two sectors.

“In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems,” the agency wrote.

Florian Schütz, the NCSC’s director, gave the first figures on Thursday. He spoke in an interview with SRF, the Swiss public broadcaster. The agency has five confirmed cases, all reported in recent days, he noted. Three targeted critical infrastructure operators, and two of those succeeded. Across all five, attackers got into systems four times.

That is one fewer than Tuesday’s advisory implied, when the agency said every known attack had worked. SRF’s report does not say why the count changed.

In Switzerland, critical infrastructure includes electricity, drinking water and telecoms suppliers, SRF reported. Attackers also hacked small and medium-sized companies, which came forward voluntarily. Schütz said there were no major outages. The NCSC will not name the victims and is leaving it to them to speak for themselves. Who is behind the attacks is still unclear.

In a recent development, the attackers used what the NCSC calls agentic offensive frameworks. These AI agents search for weaknesses on their own, pick attack tools, check the results and plan the next step. Security teams use the same tools for penetration testing.

Sources indicate that the agents exploit default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in systems connected to the internet, the agency noted. They need a fraction of the time a human attacker would. When they hit a defence, they switch to another known method. That leaves companies far less time to spot an attack and respond.

The number of such agents reachable online has almost doubled since October, according to the NCSC. It named ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI as examples. It did not say which tools the attackers used in the Swiss cases. The FBI has said ARTEX can break into networks in under three hours. This week, Microsoft said state hackers from China and North Korea now use it.

The NCSC expects more fast and successful attacks. It wants companies to install critical security updates on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release. Webmail, VPNs and other services reachable from the internet should all sit behind multi-factor authentication or passkeys. Companies should also expose as few systems as possible. The agency also shares technical indicators of these attacks with critical infrastructure operators.

“If there is no vulnerability, an AI agent cannot get into a system either,” Schütz told SRF.

Industry observers note that alex Stamos, the former Facebook security chief, mentioned this month that AI has pushed cybersecurity into a dark age. Raphael Reischuk co-founded the country’s National Test Institute for Cybersecurity and works at consulting firm Zühlke. He told SRF he expects a major wave of attacks. Many smaller companies lack the resources to keep their systems up to date, he said. He wants the federal government to consider jointly funded support for them, as it does for drinking water and electricity.

“Companies are not taking the problem seriously enough,” Reischuk stated.

#223075. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5200 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Data centers already use light in networking.
  • It has been revealed that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

It has been revealed that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

Industry observers note that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” indicates Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Recent findings suggest that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Newly introduced Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Sources indicate that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the organization’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is presently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Recent findings suggest that the most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.

According to recent reports, the argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.

Recent findings suggest that since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.

But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.

In a recent development, mcMahon indicates this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”.

It’s also vital to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.

“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”.

With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.

According to recent reports, taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

Industry observers note that the startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

Industry observers note that instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

According to recent reports, “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” states Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

Recent findings suggest that the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is presently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

In a recent development, both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr notes. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

In a recent development, free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

Industry observers note that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” notes Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

According to recent reports, “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” states Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

It has been revealed that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

In a recent development, Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the organization confirmed a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

Industry observers note that the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch states, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

It has been revealed that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the tech giant believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” indicates Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the organization’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

In a recent development, lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

Recent findings suggest that lightSolver’s team is right now working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi indicates. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

It has been revealed that yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Newly introduced says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Newly introduced, Optalysis.

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Recent findings suggest that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

In a recent development, latest says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

According to recent reports, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he indicates. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Claims Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

Breaking: Warsaw startup Lute raises $20M to build robot AI that learns from touch

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that lute, a Warsaw physical AI startup founded in January, has raised $20M to build robot models trained on touch.
  • It has been revealed that lute will spend the money on touch data, model training and latest customers.
  • Most robots and physical AI models rely on cameras alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lute team with one of its robots.

Sources indicate that lute, a Warsaw physical AI startup founded in January, has raised $20M to build robot models trained on touch. The pre-seed and seed money was confirmed on Tuesday. OTB Ventures and FORWARD.one co-led the seed round, and Credo Ventures and Seedcamp led the pre-seed. Inovo VC, Borusan Ventures, ff Venture Capital and angel investor Naval Ravikant also took part.

It has been revealed that lute will spend the money on touch data, model training and latest customers. It is hiring in Warsaw and San Mateo, California.

Most robots and physical AI models rely on cameras alone. Vision shows a robot where things are, Lute’s founders wrote. It does not show how firmly the robot holds an item, whether the item is slipping or how fragile it is.

“We believe touch is the missing signal that lets robots handle real work reliably,” chief executive Paweł Budzianowski noted in a statement published by FORWARD.one.

It has been revealed that with partners, Lute co-designed small, soft tactile sensors and built them into a portable rig. That lets it collect touch data anywhere. Zurich’s Enact is chasing the same idea, and raised $30M in October to give robots a sense of touch.

It has been revealed that lute also released its first model, Lute-0. It learns from video how a scene changes and turns that into robot movements. It is the first of a family of models Lute plans to train on touch as well as vision.

In Lute’s own retail tests, Lute-0 matched or beat π0.5, the open-source model from Physical Intelligence. It handled vegetables successfully 76% of the time, against 22% for π0.5. With soft snacks, the score was 98% against 70%. Lute notes it also responds twice as fast. The figures come from Lute’s internal evaluation, and TNW has seen no independent results.

Lute states Lute-0 was pre-trained on far less data than π0.5, and trained much faster. Its two lead investors give different figures. It used about a twentieth of the data and a quarter of the training steps, OTB Ventures wrote. FORWARD.one puts it at about a tenth of the pre-training data.

Ten months in, Lute’s models already work at what it calls Europe’s largest automotive parts distributor. OTB puts that manufacturer’s annual revenue at $6bn. Lute also works on site with large retailers, and its models run in hospital corridors, according to OTB. The startup also partners with integrators, the firms that install robots for clients, starting with healthcare and manufacturing.

In a recent development, on site, the robots work on their own where they can, and a remote operator steps in when one needs help. They run unattended about 90% of the time, according to FORWARD.one. Failures and fixes then go back into training, so each deployment improves the next.

“In physical AI, the slow and the perfect will both lose,” noted Boy de Jonge, investment manager at FORWARD.one.

Budzianowski has a machine learning PhD from Cambridge and led the machine learning team at PolyAI. He also co-founded K-Scale Labs, which built low-cost open-source humanoid robots. Co-founder Krzysztof Walas, the chief technology officer, was an associate professor at Poznań University of Technology and advised the Polish warehouse robotics company Nomagic. The team has 16 people in Warsaw and the Bay Area.

It has been revealed that bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are 45% off right now, down to $199 for Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Colors include in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Hackers breached the US Air Force’s Cloud One platform, Reuters reports

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (437 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Pentagon, headquarters of the US Department of Defense, in September 2018.
  • Hackers have broken into Cloud One, the US Air Force’s main cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday.
  • It has been revealed that two of the people remarked the intrusion came to light in the past month or so, while the system was being upgraded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pentagon, headquarters of the US Department of Defense, in September 2018.

Hackers have broken into Cloud One, the US Air Force’s main cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday. The breach could put a wide range of military data at risk, from personnel records to logistics and tactical information.

It has been revealed that two of the people remarked the intrusion came to light in the past month or so, while the system was being upgraded. Reuters could not establish who was behind it, how far it reached or whether any data was stolen.

“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the people told Reuters.

The report adds to a run of recent breaches at US government bodies, as this week, hackers hit a system used by several spy agencies, and in October a Homeland Security leak exposed 41,000 staff.

Since the discovery, work to move the Air Force’s back-office applications onto Cloud One has been paused, according to two of the sources and a fourth person. Updates to applications already running there have also been blocked, leaving staff unable to install fixes for newly disclosed flaws. A fifth person mentioned some users lost their administrator rights.

Sources indicate that another source remarked the hackers used a software flaw to reach the control plane, the layer that manages the whole platform, and compared that access to a universal remote. In theory, it could show the status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, but it is unclear whether the hackers used it that way.

The Air Force launched Cloud One in 2017 as a single home for its IT, built on cloud services from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Google. Scores of applications run on it, covering pay, personnel, logistics and maintenance.

Among them is a command-and-control system that combines air defence radar feeds from across North America, Reuters reported. Another tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force sites worldwide.

Industry observers note that SAIC ran the platform as prime contractor until Leidos took over under a $454.9M task order awarded in December 2025. According to one source, US Cyber Command has been brought in to gauge the damage, and Cyber Command did not respond either.

“[The Air Force] does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems,” the service said in a statement to Reuters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that finding the best Samsung phone is a tall order — there are so many different options available, all with the same name. It's confusing, to say the least, and finding out what sets each model apart from the others is, at best, annoying.

Sources indicate that that's why we've created this guide, so that you can more easily tell which phone is the best for you, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each. We've also made a quiz that you can use to help you find the phone that's going to fit your unique use case.

All you need to do is answer the questions, and you'll be recommended a device that fits what you want out of your next Samsung phone. It couldn't be easier. So let's get started — which is the best Samsung phone for you?

In a recent development, want to learn more about the current Samsung lineup? Here's how we rank them after thoroughly testing each model.

Recent findings suggest that while the S25 Ultra was the previous peak of Samsung's power, the Galaxy S26 Ultra arrives as a more than worthy successor. The S26 Ultra introduces a world-first "Privacy Display" that gives it a unique security advantage over every other model in Samsung's current catalog, and even phones by other brands.

However, the Ultra's Privacy Display does come with a negative: it is slightly dimmer (1,806 nits) and has narrower viewing angles than the vibrant, traditional panels found on the S25 Edge or the Z Fold 8.

Recent findings suggest that the S26 Ultra pushes the boundaries of software with its new AI powers. Samsung has added predictive tools like "Now Brief" and automated app actions that can handle complex background tasks, making it a much more capable productivity tool.

Recent findings suggest that in the photography department, the S26 Ultra remains far more advanced than any other Galaxy phone, with its 200MP main camera and 50MP telephoto lens, which have both been upgraded with wider apertures for superior low-light performance. Samsung has also introduced Horizon Lock for video, providing a level of professional-grade stabilization that the cameras on older and cheaper models cannot match.

While the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is Samsung's thinnest phone, the Galaxy S26 Ultra still managed to be thinner and lighter than its predecessor without sacrificing its 6.9-inch screen size.

Regarding battery performance, the S26 Ultra’s 16 hours and 10 minutes of life easily outclasses Samsung’s foldables like the Z Flip 7 (12:24) and Z Fold 7 (10:55). It also powers up faster thanks to newly added 60W wired charging support.

Ultimately, the S26 Ultra remains a steep $1,299 investment, especially compared to the $899 Galaxy S26. But the Ultra's combination of top-tier zoom, innovative security features, and AI-driven efficiency makes it the definitive choice for power users who find other phones simply too limited.

According to recent reports, while it's still over six inches in size (what would have been called a "phablet" not too long ago), and technically a foldable would be smaller in your pocket, the Galaxy S26 is as compact as you can get with a modern Samsung phone. And fortunately, as a flagship Galaxy S model, it's got everything you could want it to have despite its size.

The upcoming 6.3-inch AMOLED display is significantly brighter than Samsung's older models, reaching up to 1,950 nits, which makes it far more legible in direct sunlight than its predecessors or main competitors like the iPhone 17. This makes it an ideal choice for consumers who prioritize media consumption and outdoor visibility in a device that still fits comfortably in one hand.

Recent findings suggest that the S26 maintains an easy-to-carry form factor while still housing the same powerful Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset found in the more expensive Ultra model (at least in the U.S.). This ensures that average consumers get top-tier speed and gaming capabilities without the physical or financial burden of the largest devices.

It has been revealed that the introduction of new and upgraded AI features is a major selling point too. These features allow the phone to become more aware of user habits and offer sophisticated photo editing capabilities—such as generating new elements or removing reflections—that were previously limited to more niche devices. For the everyday user, these AI tools simplify complex tasks like photo editing and device management, making the smartphone experience more intuitive and efficient.

Finally, while the S26 saw a price increase to $899, it remains the most practical choice due to its high-end software experience and innovative camera features like "Horizon Lock." This video stabilization tool keeps footage perfectly level even during significant rotation, a feature the reviewer noted as being far more useful for the average person than high-resolution 8K recording. By combining professional-grade internals with user-friendly software and a manageable size, the Galaxy S26 secures its spot as the most well-rounded option in Samsung’s 2026 line-up.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is, at the moment the most expensive phone you can buy from Samsung. Apart from the ill-fated Trifold. What do you get for a $2,099 purchase? The best folding phone that you can buy right now, as you might expect. Samsung has stepped up its game with this model, after other manufacturers started to catch up and land higher places in best lists.

Industry observers note that the screen on the inside is the most noticeable improvement. For one, it’s incredibly bright and clear. This is one of the brightest AMOLED screens that Samsung has packed into a foldable yet, and it looks phenomenal. Movies are immersive, and games look epic. The crease is almost gone now too — you can still feel it with your finger, but it’s all but entirely invisible this time around.

Going back to games quickly, the Z Fold 8 Ultra is a powerhouse. We threw some very graphically intensive games at the Fold 8 Ultra, and they all ran incredibly smoothly. Gamers will love it. Productivity heads will get a kick out of it too, as they pan around and multitask without any kind of slowdown at all. This is a very powerful handset.

Recent findings suggest that we only wish that the cameras were better, especially considering how much the phone costs. The main camera is fine, and the selfie camera takes a decent image, but the telephoto camera is straight-up bad. It might as well not be there at all — everything looks blurry and awful. If you want the best camera around, you’re better off with the non-folding Galaxy S26 Ultra.

Recent findings suggest that battery life is good, with 14 and a half hours of staying power. That’s excellent, although not quite as good as the Motorola Razr Fold.

Sources indicate that and we need to talk about that price. On a phone contract, it might not be something you think about initially, but it will add up month by month. $2,099 is a lot of money for a phone, whether it's excellent or not.

“Major screen” and “easily pocketable” aren’t usually things that you’d assume could be a part of the same conversation. And yet, thanks to a very clever folding screen and square shape, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is just that. A pocketable phone with a massive screen inside. It’s about the same size and shape as a passport when it's folded.

There’s not much missing here, beyond perhaps a telephoto lens. But given how bad the telephoto lens on the more expensive Fold 8 Ultra is, it's perhaps no great loss. We’d also like it if more apps were suited to the larger screen inside, but that’s not really the fault of the phone itself. Just app developers. Still, worth thinking about if you’re going to buy one.

In a recent development, everything else is great. The large display inside is super bright and clear, and the crease in the middle has been handled with some very cool new screen tech to make it almost invisible.

The outer screen is similarly bright and clear, and easy to use with one hand thanks to that squarer shape. The whole thing is mind-blowingly thin when unfolded, as well. We really shouldn’t be wowed by stuff like this anymore, but it's hard not to be impressed by a knife-like phone in the hand.

Industry observers note that it all runs extremely smoothly as well, with the Elite chip inside handling multitasking and heavy games with ease. Gamers will love that extra screen real estate too. Productivity folks will find a lot to like too, as they hop quickly from app to app on the same screen. Very cool.

Industry observers note that cameras are fine, although by no means class-leading. If you’re looking for a camera to take loads of snaps, you’ll want one of the non-folding models. If you just want to take the occasional picture, you’ll be fine, mind you. Battery life is good too, with more than an extra hour of battery over the Fold 7. It’s likely that most consumers will be charging by the time they go to bed every evening.

In a recent development, the Fold 8 is a great phone, and this wider form factor is a master stroke that sets it apart from the larger and more expensive Fold 8 Ultra. It’s still expensive, but it hasn’t broken the $2,000 mark yet. That honor is for the flagship.

According to recent reports, the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 is a very similar phone to the 7th generation that came before it. In essence, not a necessary upgrade if you’ve got the old one. But. If you’re looking for a good flip phone to buy right now, and you’re upgrading a 3-year-old phone that’s coming up to the end of its device initiative, then there’s little better right now than the Z Flip 8.

Industry observers note that the screens this time around are brighter than ever, making sure that you can see them no matter the outside lighting conditions. Bright sun? No problem for either display in the Flip 8. There’s also some fancy latest tech in the folding display that makes the crease inside far less noticeable. Like, it’s there, but it’s far less noticeable than before.

According to recent reports, battery life is fine, although nothing to write home about. During our lab testing, we found that the phone lasted for 12 hours and 50 minutes — that’s pretty good for a folding phone, but not that much more than the previous model. Expect to be plugging in every night, regardless.

Recent findings suggest that it's smooth and slick to use thanks to a very powerful chip inside. We threw a range of different games at the phone during testing, and that larger interior display looked great the whole time. The phone had little problem running everything at high frame rates. Just don’t expect to use the outer screen. You can even use the Flip 8 as a computer with DeX, if you want. You should probably stick to your laptop.

This is an expensive phone, mind you. It comes in at around $1,099, which is more than other phones that have a similarly sized screen when it's open. For those with small pockets who sometimes want a larger screen, though, you’ll love the Flip 8.

According to recent reports, the Samsung Galaxy A57 stands out as Samsung’s best value phone this year, delivering an expansive 6.7-inch display at a midrange price that’s especially compelling for buyers who want big-screen utility without overspending. The screen size brings benefits for streaming and multitasking, and the price means you don’t have to compromise on core features.

It has been revealed that battery life is a clear highlight, with the A57 using a battery as large as the S26 Ultra. Long-term value is another strength. Samsung guarantees six years of security updates and four years of major Android upgrades, so buyers can expect their investment to stay secure and current well past the average upgrade cycle. It's not as good as the seven-year offer you get with a flagship Samsung, but still plenty of time.

Sources indicate that compared to Samsung’s upmarket S26 Ultra and S26, the A57 lacks some luxuries. It doesn’t come with the S26 Ultra’s brighter display, ultra-fast performance, or advanced AI camera features. For hundreds less, you still get a roomy screen and reliable everyday camera performance — essentials most consumers genuinely need.

In a recent development, the Galaxy A57 is our pick for buyers who want a long-lasting phone with a big screen and great battery life but don’t need the latest in AI tricks or flagship camera prowess. If you want a future-proof everyday workhorse at a sensible price, this is the Samsung to get. Those chasing cutting-edge AI or the brightest, fastest display may want to look at the S26 Ultra instead.

According to recent reports, in previous years, the cheaper FE edition of the flagship would easily outperform the A-edition. But this time around, the S26 FE isn't quite a step up from the S25 FE, and the A57 is a significant improvement on the A56. The S26 FE is still almost twice the price of the A57, but the gap between them is shrinking.

One thing the S26 FE does have is a lot of AI features. Some are good, most are novelties, but if you need a more affordable entry-point to Samsung's tools, this is the phone to go for. Not that it always feels it (and I mean that literally). The materials in the 2026 model don't have the same premium quality.

It has been revealed that then again, it doesn't feel like a cheap phone, which often are quite plastic-y in your hand. Whether this is an appropriate compromise when this isn't actually a cheap-cheap phone depends on how far your budget will stretch to get access to Samsung's latest features, when the A57 isn't far behind, performance-wise.

Industry observers note that at the time of writing, we've not been able to perform our full battery tests, so can't accurately compare it against the other models. But it seems about in line with past FE performance; good, not great. Enough to see you through a day, but you'll still need a charger handy by the evening or a few hours of heavy use.

If I seem a little down on the Galaxy S26 FE, I'm not. It's a very good phone with a lot of what we liked about the mainline S26 at a cheaper price. But the A57 isn't a whole lot different and is quite a bit cheaper, so I have a hard time recommending this phone when there's a more bank-balance-friendly option available.

Sources indicate that picking which Samsung phone to buy is primarily driven by budget considerations. You won't want to look at the latest Galaxy S Ultra or Z Fold if you're not prepared to pay for it. But other factors need to be taken into consideration as well.

According to recent reports, focusing on battery life will mean ruling out Samsung's foldables. Most other phones on this list have strong longevity on a single charge, but unfortunately, you'll probably have to pay more to get the best available battery life.

It has been revealed that for photography, the best will normally be the latest Galaxy S Ultra model. That goes for productivity too, due to Samsung bundling the S Pen in with its Ultra models, unless you'd prefer the extra screen space and multitasking options that a Galaxy Z Fold can provide. And if you're a gamer, any Galaxy S phone will offer the best possible performance — it's just up to you to decide how much you want to pay for other features on top of that.

For a smartphone to make our best phone list, it needs to excel on several tests that we run on every handset. We perform some of these tests in our labs and some in the real world. See our detailed explanation on how Tom's Guide tests and reviews smartphones for more information.

Industry observers note that when it comes to performance, we rely on such synthetic benchmarks as Geekbench 6 and 3DMark to measure graphics performance. These tests allow us to compare performance across iPhones and Android devices.

In a recent development, we also run a real-world video transcoding test on each phone using the Adobe Premiere Rush app and time the result. (We unfortunately have to skip this test on some phones due to app compatibility challenges, but we attempt this benchmark with each device we get in to review.).

Geekbench 6 (single-core / multicore).

To measure the quality of a phone's display, we perform lab tests to determine the brightness of the panel (in nits), as well as how colorful each screen is (DCI-P3 color gamut). In these cases, higher numbers are better. We also measure the color accuracy of each panel with a Delta-E rating, where lower numbers are better, and a score of 0 is perfect.

One of the most important tests we run is the Tom's Guide battery test. We run a web surfing test over 5G (or 4G if the phone doesn't have 5G support) at 150 nits of screen brightness until the battery gives out. In general, a phone that lasts 10 hours or more is good, and anything above 11 hours makes our list of the best phone battery life.

Last but not least, we take the best phones out in the field to take photos outdoors, indoors, and at night in low light to see how they perform versus their closest competitors.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none.
  • It has been revealed that 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.

Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.

Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.

It has been revealed that 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.

According to recent reports, auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.

Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.

Incognito: see the Incognito section above.

Sources indicate that reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.

yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay concern that the mirror has by default.

Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver).

Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage.

Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL.

Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes.

Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops.

Sources indicate that safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):.

Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.

Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:.

Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.

In a recent development, youTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.

According to recent reports, if millions of consumers did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that indicates "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.

"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator.

It has been revealed that best combo: uBlock Origin (blocks most ads) + 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher (catches the ones that slip through and logs them) + SponsorBlock (skips sponsor reads). They don't conflict.

MIT — do whatever you want with it.

Built with Alice (SIFTA) for George Anton.

"If millions installed this, YouTube would feel every reload." 🐜.
