📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SAP’s headquarters building in Walldorf, Germany, with the company logo on its roof.

SAP has confirmed a security incident after it spotted suspicious activity in its systems.

In a statement issued on Thursday evening, the German software company said that, so far, it has found no sign that anyone got into customer business data.

Der Spiegel first reported the incident on Thursday, describing it as a hacking attack, and according to an insider who spoke to the magazine, attackers stole access tokens from SAP employees.

The attackers then used the tokens to copy and change SAP source code on GitHub, the insider noted. Citing internal sources, Der Spiegel added that the attackers may have used agentic AI, meaning AI tools that can carry out tasks on their own.

Sources indicate that according to the magazine, SAP is treating it internally as an active security incident under the codename Project Granite. The manufacturer has not confirmed the token theft or the changes to its code.

“SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers,” the organization stated.

However, SAP did not say what kind of activity it found, when it was discovered or which parts of the business were affected, the German news agency dpa reported.

The incident came to light on the same day that reports said SAP is weighing at least 10,000 job cuts as it reorganises around AI.

According to recent reports, attackers have also gone after SAP’s developer tools earlier this year. In April, criminals hijacked four SAP packages on npm, a large public store of JavaScript code, and used them to spread malware that steals passwords and keys.

Recent findings suggest that the bad versions were online for only a few hours, but the packages are downloaded more than 550,000 times a week, according to Heise. Security researchers linked that attack to a group called TeamPCP.

Meanwhile, Germany’s cybersecurity agency, the BSI, issued a public warning on Thursday about AI attack tools that can act on their own, naming ARTEX, CAIRN and PentAGI.

Meanwhile, in the US, an AI hacking tool is also believed to have been used against several spy agencies in a breach that came to light this week.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (908 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Judge orders Apple to produce 3,200 documents in Epic Games dispute

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A federal judge has ordered Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents for Epic Games to review, following Epic’s allegations that Apple improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • With Apple and Epic trading arguments in the Supreme Court over whether the civil contempt ruling against Apple should stand, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • In August, Apple submitted its proposal to the district court, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A federal judge has ordered Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents for Epic Games to review, following Epic’s allegations that Apple improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

With Apple and Epic trading arguments in the Supreme Court over whether the civil contempt ruling against Apple should stand, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

In August, Apple submitted its proposal to the district court, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%. Epic, however, is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

Earlier this month, Epic accused Apple of improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching a set of search terms agreed upon by both companies to help identify documents that could shed light on how Apple arrived at those rates.

[…] Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s fresh CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness.

Apple, in turn, pushed back against Epic’s accusations, saying the search terms were overly broad and had captured large numbers of documents unrelated to the proceedings.

Sources indicate that […] at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms […]. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The firm also asked the court to reject Epic’s motion to order it to produce all non-privileged documents matching the agreed-upon search terms, and alternatively suggested submitting a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deemed nonresponsive to a Special Master for independent review.

As it turns out, neither manufacturer got exactly what it originally wanted, but the judge ruled largely in Epic’s favor on how to determine whether Apple had improperly withheld documents.

Following a hearing in which both companies presented their respective proposals for how a randomized sampling of the documents should be conducted, Magistrate Judge Thomas S. Hixson decided to adopt Epic’s proposal, which called for Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents it had previously deemed nonresponsive, along with their associated document families, for Epic itself to review.

All documents in the sample will be drawn from the files of the seven Apple custodians referenced in Epic’s original motion.

Apple, by contrast, had suggested a considerably smaller sample of 383 documents, arguing that this would be statistically significant at a 95% confidence level.

In his decision, Judge Hixson agreed that Epic had legitimate reasons to question Apple’s reasons for withholding the documents:.

Apple’s responsiveness rate is so dramatically low that it raises red flags. With Apple screening out more than 99% of the documents that hit on the agreed search terms, it is unreasonable to ask Epic to believe that Apple is making these responsiveness calls in good faith. That is particularly true in this case, in which Judge Gonzalez Rogers has sanctioned Apple for its large-scale abuse of the attorney-client privilege for the purpose of obscuring the evidence.

Judge Hixson also rejected Apple’s suggestion that a Special Master conduct the review, arguing that given the level of familiarity with the case required to assess the relevance of these documents, Epic was the only practical option for determining whether Apple had systematically misclassified them.

Realistically, the only person who has the practical ability to determine if Apple has been systematically mis-coding documents as nonresponsive is its opponent, Epic.

In his decision, the judge agreed with Apple that the organization should be allowed to review the documents for privileged and sensitive information before producing them to Epic, and authorized Apple to designate all documents produced as part of the exercise as Attorneys’ Eyes Only.

Importantly, Judge Hixson has not yet determined whether Apple systematically misclassified responsive documents as nonresponsive, nor has he imposed the daily monetary sanctions originally requested by Epic.

Apple now has until December 8 to complete the document production, with Epic having until December 15 to file any objections, and Apple until December 22 to respond.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Recent findings suggest that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash latest competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

Industry observers note that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

It has been revealed that RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

It has been revealed that recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company revealed a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

In a recent development, but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. It has been revealed that claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

It has been revealed that finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

In a recent development, pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

In a recent development, there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

In a recent development, but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

It has been revealed that A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

Sources indicate that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s crucial to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Sources indicate that last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

Sources indicate that to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a newly introduced instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

In a recent development, these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Recent findings suggest that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

According to recent reports, in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Recent findings suggest that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

It has been revealed that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its consumers because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

It has been revealed that the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Industry observers note that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the manufacturer judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

It has been revealed that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Industry observers note that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Worksinprogress

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan.
  • Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College.
  • Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.

Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’.

Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build upcoming, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Recent findings suggest that through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture. Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’.

In the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’.

Recent findings suggest that the loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, notable details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’.

In a recent development, mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As they tell me, “This has not been done for 300 years!” So, it was a great experience, a voyage of discovery, so much that we learnt from each other.’.

It is my great pleasure to introduce our readers to one of the most skilled and thoughtful architects working today.

Now in his mid-eighties, Mumtaz continues to build. ‘It does feel like you’ve set the foundations for an alternative approach to contemporary urban environments’, an interviewer recently suggested to him. ‘I’m just keeping my fingers crossed! No idea what will happen’, Mumtaz replied.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, two Chinese companies installed Nvidia’s restricted Blackwell chips at a Shanghai data centre linked to Alice Huang, Bloomberg reported on Friday.
  • It has been revealed that the filings show for the first time that Blackwell chips reached the site, the Yangtze River Delta Project, Bloomberg stated.
  • It has been revealed that shanghai Shuoyao pledged a GB300 NVL72 rack, one of Nvidia’s most powerful products, to secure a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, two Chinese companies installed Nvidia’s restricted Blackwell chips at a Shanghai data centre linked to Alice Huang, Bloomberg reported on Friday. Reporters Andy Lin, Mackenzie Hawkins and Kari Soo Lindberg found the evidence in loan documents that companies submitted to Chinese regulators.

It has been revealed that the filings show for the first time that Blackwell chips reached the site, the Yangtze River Delta Project, Bloomberg stated. Shipping Blackwell to China has always required a US licence.

It has been revealed that shanghai Shuoyao pledged a GB300 NVL72 rack, one of Nvidia’s most powerful products, to secure a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank. The rack’s serial number appeared in documents submitted in November.

Bloomberg ran that number through a public warranty database. It showed that Taiwan’s Gigabyte built the rack. Gigabyte assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks, and it declined to say who it first sold the hardware to, citing company policy.

The organization “conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” a Gigabyte spokesperson told Bloomberg in an emailed statement.

Sources indicate that A second firm, Shanghai Kezhan, described a GB200 server, which also uses Blackwell chips, at the same site. It did so when it took a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a leasing firm that a Shanghai government agency owns. Kezhan also listed 32 servers with H200 chips, an earlier restricted Nvidia model.

How the GB300 rack reached China, or the site, is unclear. Such gear often passes through several hands, and sellers often first ship smuggled products to places without restrictions, Bloomberg said.

It has been revealed that alice Huang founded Megaspeed in 2023. The Singapore tech giant became Nvidia’s largest customer in Southeast Asia and is under US investigation over suspected chip smuggling. The US blacklisted Megaspeed this week, and then Alibaba’s Singapore unit.

Shuoyao is active at the Shanghai site and overlaps significantly with Megaspeed, according to Bloomberg. This month it confirmed it is one of Megaspeed’s service providers.

Shuoyao described the partnership as “limited to ordinary commercial cooperation”.

Recent findings suggest that megaspeed used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to show investors its largest data centre, according to Bloomberg. Huang also has ties to several companies that invested in the project. NeXPower Japan, which the Chinese outlet Caixin mentioned Huang controls, owns 83.3% of Kezhan.

It has been revealed that bloomberg remarked it has no evidence that Megaspeed itself sent Nvidia hardware to the site. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in the US probe, and neither Megaspeed nor Nvidia answered Bloomberg’s questions about the project.

Industry observers note that local media have mentioned the site could house up to 800,000 servers. That would put it on a par with the facilities OpenAI uses. The filings cover only hardware pledged for loans, so they show a small part of what is there, Bloomberg said. They also show that some Chinese lenders, including ones with government ties, lent money against restricted chips.

In a recent development, the report lands days after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, amid scrutiny of how its chips reach China. President Donald Trump has mentioned he does not want Blackwell chips going to China. Huang once said a GB300 rack, which weighs more than 1,500 kilograms, was too major to smuggle.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (525 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Papa John’s AI agent pays by bank, not card, in TrueLayer’s FCA pilot

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Francesco Simoneschi, co-founder and CEO of TrueLayer.
  • In a recent development, an AI agent at Papa John’s has paid for a customer’s order straight from their bank account, with no card.
  • It has been revealed that the test ran with UK banks including Lloyds and NatWest, inside the Financial Conduct Authority’s Supercharged Sandbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Francesco Simoneschi, co-founder and CEO of TrueLayer.

In a recent development, an AI agent at Papa John’s has paid for a customer’s order straight from their bank account, with no card. TrueLayer calls it the first agentic Pay by Bank payment to a named UK retailer. The London payments organization announced the pilot on Friday, the day of Black Friday sales.

It has been revealed that the test ran with UK banks including Lloyds and NatWest, inside the Financial Conduct Authority’s Supercharged Sandbox. TrueLayer presented what it learned to the regulator and the industry at the FCA’s showcase on 26 November. The order itself was nine mini margherita pizzas, the Guardian reported.

The customer links a bank account, not a card, to their Papa John’s account through open banking. Papa John’s AI agent helps with the order and then requests the payment from that account.

When linking the account, the customer sets spending limits with their bank, per merchant or over a set period. The bank checks every payment against those limits and declines anything above them, so the agent cannot overspend. The customer approves inside their bank app, and the agent never sees bank logins or passwords. The customer can cancel the arrangement from the merchant or the banking app at any time.

According to recent reports, the payments use variable recurring payment (VRP) connections, which let a provider take repeated payments of different amounts under one approval. TrueLayer said the pilot was the first time Lloyds’ and NatWest’s VRP systems were used for agentic payments.

In a recent development, trueLayer argues that bank payments suit AI agents better than cards, because shoppers can set limits with their bank without sharing card details. It also states non-card payments can keep competition alive in how merchants accept money as agents take on more shopping.

“Agents will choose the payment rail that is fastest, most secure and lowest cost, not the one people use out of habit,” said Francesco Simoneschi, TrueLayer’s chief executive and co-founder, in the announcement.

“Today it’s pizza. Tomorrow it’s everything else,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that the rival model is already on sale in the UK. Meta’s Muse agent released there this week and pays with a customer’s card. Meta also declined an FCA test of Muse in the same regulatory programme.

The Papa John’s payment remains a pilot, not a service open to all customers. TrueLayer mentioned the showcase will feed into the conditions and standards needed to use the technology safely at scale.

The timing matters for every organization building agents that move money. On 24 November the FCA warned AI agent builders that existing rules apply to them and that some may need its authorisation.

According to recent reports, simoneschi and Luca Martinetti founded TrueLayer in 2016. The manufacturer indicates more than 30 million people in 22 countries use its network. It processes more than $150bn in payments a year, the company said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Readdle updated its Documents app for iPhone and iPad this week with Voice Notes, a newly introduced AI-powered feature that lets customers record conversations and automatically generate transcripts, summaries, and follow-up notes. Here are the details.

While the habit of recording meetings, lectures, or even one’s own thoughts is not particularly fresh, modern AI tools and models have made it considerably easier to extract useful information from these recordings without having to listen back to them in their entirety or take copious notes that can distract from the actual conversation.

This week, Readdle’s Documents introduced Voice Notes, which “lets you record audio and turn it into a summary, follow-ups, and a full transcript,” as the manufacturer put it.

People can start a latest recording session by tapping the “+” button in the app and selecting Voice Notes. Alternatively, they can start recording from the iPhone’s Action button, which is a nice touch.

Once they’re done, Readdle notes Documents can generate:.

People can cycle through these three tabs, where they can also listen to the original recording or copy and share the information.

Readdle claims Voice Notes can recognize multiple languages in the same conversation, with the actual transcript preserving the languages as spoken, “while the summary and follow-ups are generated in the most frequently spoken language.”.

Each voice note is saved as a single file in Documents that contains the original recording, transcript, summary, and follow-ups. Customers can organize these files into folders, share them, sync them with their cloud storage, and save the transcript as a separate .txt file.

However, if users give a voice note’s AI-generated content a thumbs down, Readdle may retain its transcript and summary for up to six months, or until the user objects to their processing, whichever comes first.

The manufacturer also indicates user data isn’t used to train AI models, although third-party AI providers may retain inputs for up to 30 days for abuse and misuse monitoring, or longer if required by law.

#223049. Industry News: Latest York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1420 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eff ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Latest York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eff

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different.
  • EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts.
  • Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young owners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for Fresh York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young owners. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

Recent findings suggest that for example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

It has been revealed that along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the Upcoming York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

In a recent development, the New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

According to recent reports, echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in Upcoming York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

In a recent development, under both states' regimes, many people will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

According to recent reports, when young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

In a recent development, legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, Newly introduced York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.

According to recent reports, take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

It has been revealed that if these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet people meaningful choice and control.

  • Recent findings suggest that poland signed the contract on Friday.
  • Poland’s defence ministry signed a contract with Palantir Technologies on Friday to buy Maven Smart System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz during talks at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., in May 2025.

Recent findings suggest that poland signed the contract on Friday. The five-year deal for Palantir’s Maven Smart System is worth an estimated $300M. The defence minister gave the figure, Bloomberg reported. This article has been updated with the signing, the value and the minister’s comments.

Poland’s defence ministry signed a contract with Palantir Technologies on Friday to buy Maven Smart System. The AI software helps armed forces analyse battlefield data and make decisions. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz put the five-year deal’s estimated value at about $300M, Bloomberg reported.

It has been revealed that the ministry unveiled the signing on Thursday, Reuters reported, citing a ministry statement. The contract is with Palantir’s Polish subsidiary. NATO and the US military already use the same system. Palantir has remarked it cannot switch off NATO’s Maven system.

According to recent reports, kosiniak-Kamysz called the deal historic when he spoke to reporters in Warsaw. He stated Poland would be the sole owner of the system’s data and infrastructure.

Poland will own the “keys, servers and information” under the agreement, Kosiniak-Kamysz said, according to Bloomberg.

“Whenever possible, we choose a Polish product,” he said. Where no Polish system has comparable capabilities, the ministry picks the best one in the world, he added.

Palantir has not commented publicly on the deal or its terms.

Recent findings suggest that the contract is the first binding step in a partnership that began with a cybersecurity agreement in December 2024. In October 2025, the minister and Palantir chief executive Alex Karp signed a letter of intent covering AI, IT and cybersecurity. At that signing, the minister said testing had begun in December 2023. It included dozens of meetings, exercises and demonstrations across all branches of the armed forces.

In a recent development, the deal has drawn opposition at home. Protesters gathered in Warsaw earlier this month over security and data privacy. The activist group Nasze Dane also asked Poland’s human rights ombudsman to examine the cooperation.

According to recent reports, the ombudsman, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, wrote to the minister in October about the group’s concerns. She asked how the ministry had assessed the privacy risks. In early November, Kosiniak-Kamysz told broadcaster RMF FM he was waiting for the military to finish its analysis.

According to recent reports, poland’s Cyberspace Defence Forces Component Command led the negotiations. The minister has defended the choice by pointing out that NATO and Ukraine’s armed forces already use Palantir’s software.

Poland is moving in the opposite direction to some of its allies. France and Germany have pledged to build a European Palantir rival, and Germany is testing 30 AI tools for its military. The Netherlands wants a full replacement for the firm’s software within two years.

It has been revealed that warsaw has also been deepening defence technology ties with Washington. Earlier this week, Poland and the US signed an agreement at the Pentagon on joint defence research and development, ending 17 years of negotiations.

Recent findings suggest that terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also shows how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple’s share of US smartphone shipments jumped from 50% to 57% year over year last quarter, with the company being the only major smartphone maker to buck the broader trend of declining shipments. Here are the details.

Industry observers note that yesterday, we covered a Counterpoint Research report on Q3 Latin American smartphone shipments, which demonstrated Apple recording the smallest year-over-year decline among the region’s top five smartphone makers. As a result, Apple increased its share of regional shipments from 7% to 9%.

The report echoed the findings of several others published throughout this year, which showed how Apple has managed to navigate component shortages and rising costs better than many of its competitors, some of which have had to raise smartphone prices multiple times.

Apple, by contrast, kept iPhone pricing largely stable for much of the year, holding off on broader price increases until the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro lineup in September.

Today, Counterpoint Research released its report on US smartphone shipments for Q3, which showed that Apple increased its share from 50% to 57% year over year, amid a 9% decline in overall shipments.

According to a separate Counterpoint report published last Thursday, Apple was the only major smartphone maker to avoid a year-over-year decline in shipment volume during the quarter.

In today’s report, Counterpoint notes that rising memory costs hit the low-end Android segment particularly hard during the quarter. Samsung was the only major Android smartphone maker to increase its shipment share, seeing a one-percentage-point bump to 25%, “helped by a portfolio spanning flagships and the low-end Galaxy A-series.”.

Carriers also felt the impact of the broader downturn, with smartphone sales across the three major US carriers collectively falling 4% year over year, per the report.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects memory costs to remain elevated and US carriers to be more selective with their holiday promotions, with smartphone sales expected to remain weak in Q4 despite it typically being the strongest quarter of the year.

Belgium’s Wallonia halts Google data centre after permit was revoked

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.
  • The Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium.
  • It has been revealed that about 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.

The Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium. Work had carried on for months at the site in Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles without a valid permit. The order came on Thursday, days after Greenpeace Belgium asked the regional government to step in.

It has been revealed that about 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT. The Walloon infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, had announced an investigation on Wednesday.

Google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centres cooled by air. In 2025 the company changed its plans. It merged two of the buildings into one larger building and switched to cooling with water from the Sambre river, Greenpeace noted.

Recent findings suggest that the Walloon administration approved that amended permit in April 2026. After residents appealed, Desquesnes revoked it in August. The request covered 600 cubic metres of river water an hour, the minister remarked. Less than a quarter of it would have gone back into the river, according to Belga.

In a recent development, residents then told Greenpeace that work was still going on. The group investigated, using satellite images, and launched an emergency procedure earlier this week.

“Tech giants are not above the law,” said Nadia Cornejo, a Greenpeace Belgium spokesperson. “This should already have been the case in August, when the permit was cancelled.”.

Google appealed the revocation but did not wait for the court to rule before carrying on with the work, VRT reported.

Google is committed to “an open and collaborative dialogue with the regional government and experts” on its investments in Wallonia, a spokesperson told VRT.

On 17 October it asked Belgium’s Council of State to annul and suspend the minister’s decision. Greenpeace and several residents asked to join the case on 16 November, and a public hearing is set for 7 January.

It has been revealed that data centres have faced similar local opposition elsewhere. Google’s Finnish data centre project drew a police investigation, and residents in Indonesia’s Batam protested over water in October. In the US, voters rejected data centre measures at the midterms.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) revealed today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup.
  • Back in March 2025, shortly after Apple declared it was delaying the rollout of what would eventually become Siri AI, the South Korean civic group Seoul YMCA filed a complaint with the KFTC.
  • At the time, Yonhap reported that the organization had previously called on Apple to compensate affected customers, and alleged that the firm may have continued to market the iPhone 16 lineup despite already knowing that some of its advertised AI features would be delayed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) revealed today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Here are the details.

Back in March 2025, shortly after Apple declared it was delaying the rollout of what would eventually become Siri AI, the South Korean civic group Seoul YMCA filed a complaint with the KFTC.

At the time, Yonhap reported that the organization had previously called on Apple to compensate affected customers, and alleged that the firm may have continued to market the iPhone 16 lineup despite already knowing that some of its advertised AI features would be delayed.

As 9to5Mac readers will likely remember, Apple widely advertised Apple Intelligence and AI-powered Siri features as part of its iPhone 16 launch campaign, going so far as to give its iconic Fifth Avenue store an Apple Intelligence-themed makeover and run an ad campaign starring Bella Ramsey.

This landed Apple in legal and regulatory trouble in multiple markets, including the US, where the company agreed to a $250 million class action settlement earlier this year, and Brazil, where it came under scrutiny from a consumer protection agency in May. Now, the company is facing potential penalties in South Korea as well.

Industry observers note that as a result of Seoul YMCA’s complaint, the KFTC conducted an investigation into Apple’s advertising practices. Today, the regulator announced (via MacRumors) that its investigators had submitted their findings and recommendations for formal deliberation by the Commission.

According to the KFTC’s press release, investigators concluded that Apple advertised Apple Intelligence and its planned staggered rollout on the iPhone 16 website, but “concealed, downplayed, or omitted information material to consumers’ purchasing decisions.”.

That included, per the press release (translation ours):.

The press release also notes that Genmoji, Image Playground, “Siri with the ability to understand personal context,” and “Siri that provides step-by-step guidance” were not made available as advertised:.

For example, Siri’s ability to understand personal context was advertised as being scheduled to launch first in US English by the end of 2024, as currently available in US English in October 2024, and as scheduled to support Korean in early April 2025.

In reality, the feature was not released in US English until September 2026, with Korean language support following in October 2026.

As a result, the investigators concluded that Apple’s conduct constituted a violation of the country’s Labeling and Advertising Act, which prohibits deceptive labeling and advertising.

They recommended issuing corrective orders, including a prohibition on such conduct in the future, as well as imposing a financial penalty.

They also estimate that Apple’s revenue associated with the alleged violation amounts to approximately 3.35 trillion South Korean won (roughly $2.5 billion), though the KFTC’s press release does not specify the amount of the fine.

⁠Yonhap noted today that the fine could reach roughly $48 million, while ⁠KBS reported that it could range between $21 million and $42 million.

With the report now submitted, Apple has six weeks to submit its written defense before the Commission deliberates and makes a final determination on whether the firm violated the law and, if so, how much it should be fined.

According to recent reports, in a statement to MacRumors, Apple noted it had cooperated with the KFTC’s investigation, but disagreed with the conclusions. The manufacturer also highlighted the rollout of Korean-language support for Apple Intelligence last year and, more recently, for Siri AI.

Industry observers note that if you’re anything like me, you know the exact spiral that hits when your to-do list gets overwhelming. Your brain panics, you bounce between six smaller distractions to feel “productive,” and by 5 PM, you’ve somehow been busy all day while finishing absolutely nothing.

That’s why I was equal parts skeptical and desperate when I slipped on the Neurable One — a pair of over-ear ANC headphones that pack 12 EEG sensors directly into the ear cushions to read your brainwave patterns in real time.

Normally $499, Neurable has knocked $50 off for Black Friday, dropping them to $449 through November 30 — and crucially, there’s no subscription paywall locked behind the app. After testing them myself, I can confirm they genuinely work.

Save $50 on these brain-sensing ANC headphones that pack 12 dry EEG sensors into great-sounding 40mm beryllium drivers to track your focus, flag burnout before it hits, and keep you on task — with zero monthly subscription fees.

Sources indicate that first, let’s clear up the sci-fi paranoia: these aren’t reading your thoughts. The fabric sensors knitted into the memory foam pads pick up electrical patterns from your brain (no messy gel or electrodes required) and translate them into a live Focus Tracking feed and a Brain battery fuel gauge in the companion app.

Recent findings suggest that for a serial procrastinator (hi), having a live scoreboard for your attention is a game-changer. Starting a focus session turns staying on task into a literal workout for your brain: you can see the exact moment your concentration starts to drift, and the app nudges you to take Smart Brain Breaks before you hit the wall and doomscroll for an hour.

Industry observers note that since I started working with these on, I’m noticeably getting more done in my day without feeling fried by the evening. But the weirdest, most welcome side effect? My sleep score actually improved too — likely because I’m finally respecting my mental bandwidth during work hours instead of trying to brute force through exhaustion.

Normally, some party trick comes at the cost of forgetting to make a good pair of headphones. Fortunately, Neurable’s first all-in-house design gets the audio fundamentals right.

The custom 40mm beryllium drivers sound crisp, balanced and genuinely enjoyable for long workdays — tuned for clean, fatigue-free listening rather than bloated showroom bass.

According to recent reports, yes, the companion app’s EQ options are limited, which is going to bug the hardcore audio tweakers out there. But to my trained ears, the out-the-box audio quality is strong enough that it’s nowhere near a dealbreaker.

You also get solid active noise cancellation, a clear latency-free ambient mode and Bluetooth multipoint for hopping between your laptop and phone.

Before you do buy, I’d be doing a disservice in not pointing out a couple of downsides with these cans:.

At $449, the Neurable one is still a serious investment — and if you just want the absolute lightest travel headphones with the greatest sound quality, there are plenty of mainstream options.

But if you struggle with distraction, burnout, or juggling ten half-finished tasks at once, these are the rare wellness wearable that actually earns its keep.

Getting a great sounding pair of ANC headphones and a personal focus coach for $50 off — with zero monthly fees — makes this one of the most interesting pair of cans I’ve tested this year, and my personal favorite Black Friday deal.
